data.name: Finding.Memory.XmpOnWithUncleanShutdowns
data.value: Overclock on and unclean shutdowns in the last 90 days. Your RAM runs above the JEDEC standard speed: it is a memory overclock, by XMP/EXPO profile or manual setting, and the BIOS domain says which when it is readable; and Windows has restarted without a clean shutdown (long presses of the power button excluded; the breakdown, blue screens included, is in the stability report). DrDXT has not tested this setting and is not blaming it. Why go back to JEDEC: it is the only way to know whether this overclock crashes the machine. It tests stability, not performance. Stay on JEDEC for at least three times the usual gap between two shutdowns: for example, with one shutdown every nine days, a week without one can happen by chance. If the shutdowns stop over that time, the overclock becomes the most likely suspect. If they continue, the overclock is not the cause, but the modules are not cleared either. A memory test checks them faster than weeks of waiting: the one built into Windows (Windows + R, then mdsched.exe; it restarts the PC and keeps it busy during the test), whose result DrDXT then shows in the stability report, or MemTest86, which takes longer. Without restarting, the test in the Act section below checks a quarter of your memory in five minutes, but it cannot see the memory Windows itself uses: no error is not the same as a full test.

data.name: tweak.fixit.pagefile_ssd.title
data.value: Page file handed back to the system drive (SSD)

data.name: tweak.fixit.pagefile_ssd.summary
data.value: Your page file is on a hard drive while Windows is on an SSD: everything that spills out of memory (loading, back to the desktop) goes through the slow drive. DrDXT hands its management back to Windows, the same value as "Automatically manage" in the virtual memory settings, and Windows puts it back on the system drive. Takes effect at the next restart. Reliability and smoothness, no extra frames claimed. Reversible: Undo puts back the previous location.

data.name: tweak.fixit.plan_economie.title
data.value: Power saver plan set back to Balanced

data.name: tweak.fixit.plan_economie.summary
data.value: Your desktop PC is on the Power saver plan, which tunes the processor to use little power: for gaming, that is the wrong way. DrDXT switches back to Balanced, Windows' default plan (and the only one that carries the Windows 11 power mode slider). No frame gain is published for this change: your matches will show what it brings. Reversible: Undo brings back Power saver.

data.name: tweak.fixit.wifi_performances.title
data.value: Wi-Fi card taken out of power saving

data.name: tweak.fixit.wifi_performances.summary
data.value: Your game goes through Wi-Fi and your power plan keeps the wireless card in power saving mode on AC: Microsoft says this mode "reduces power consumption at the cost of increased data transfer latency" (the card skips beacons and wakes up to send). DrDXT sets this single value to "Maximum Performance", on AC, in your active plan; the battery value is left alone. No extra frames: fewer ping spikes. The next scan shows the jitter to your router. Reversible. The real fix is still a cable.

data.name: tweak.fixit.cpu_power_cap.title
data.value: Power cap against heat

data.name: tweak.fixit.cpu_power_cap.summary
data.value: Your last game was held back by heat while your motherboard lets the processor draw far more than the game needs. DrDXT caps the sustained limit (PL1): what your game drew at its median, plus a third. The game runs the same, only the long hot peaks are cut; the few-second bursts (PL2) stay in the BIOS. The doctor reads your next games and tells whether the processor is held back less. "Undo" puts the old limit back, and nothing is kept across a reboot: the BIOS restores its value.

data.name: tweak.fixit.cpu_power_limit.title
data.value: Processor power limit raised

data.name: tweak.fixit.cpu_power_limit.summary
data.value: Your motherboard holds the processor under a sustained power limit (PL1) lower than the peak it already allows (PL2): in game it holds its clocks for a few seconds, then drops. DrDXT raises the sustained limit up to that peak, nothing beyond what the board already allows, and never voltage or current. Measured by TechPowerUp on a 14900K: a 65 W limit costs about 15% of frames at 1080p; 125 W, 2% (https://www.techpowerup.com/review/intel-core-i9-14900k-raptor-lake-tested-at-power-limits-down-to-35-w/). DrDXT judges it on your games, in blocks of with, without, without, with, and puts the old limit back unless it clearly gains. The processor runs hotter when held higher: it throttles itself at its maximum temperature. Nothing is kept across a reboot: the BIOS restores its value.

data.name: tweak.fixit.mode_boost.summary
data.value: Processor boost is turned off in your power plan (plugged in), while that plan's default allows it: the processor no longer goes above its base clock. DrDXT sets your plan's default value back, nothing else (battery is not touched). The gain is not known in advance: DrDXT measures it in a game and puts the old setting back if it gains nothing. Reversible. On a 13th or 14th generation Intel, a boost turned off can be a choice, against heat: turned off on purpose? Leave it.

data.value: Resizable BAR is off. Intel states ReBAR is required for optimal Arc performance: the card runs without it, but under-performs. Enable it in the BIOS/UEFI (Re-Size BAR / Smart Access Memory), with CSM disabled and UEFI boot on.

data.name: Finding.Gpu.IntelDriverIsTheLever
data.value: On Arc, the graphics driver is by far the biggest real lever: Intel ships game-ready drivers with per-title optimisations, and DX9/DX11 titles gain the most. DrDXT cannot judge how far behind an Arc driver is, its freshness floor is too coarse for Intel's release cadence, so check it yourself.

data.name: Finding.Network.RssOff
data.value: Receive Side Scaling (RSS) is off on this adapter. Microsoft recommends keeping it ON: it spreads network processing across CPU cores instead of pinning it to one. Enable it in the adapter's advanced properties.

data.name: Finding.Display.MixedRefreshIdlePower
data.value: Your displays run at different refresh rates. On some NVIDIA cards this can stop the video memory from dropping into its idle state: the clock stays high, and so does power draw, permanently, not just while you play. NVIDIA support once called this intended for several high refresh displays on an older card, and suggested going below 144 Hz outside games; nothing confirms your card behaves the same: it is yours to try. What we do not promise: a number. The reported savings come from other machines. Try it on the second display only: never on the gaming one, that would cost you frames. Another possible cause: an application accelerated by the card (browser, Discord, launchers) can also keep it awake. To tell which one it is on your machine, close them and compare.

data.name: Finding.Network.LinkPowerSavingOn
data.value: A link power-saving feature is active on this adapter (green ethernet, power saving mode, or 802.3az). The link goes idle when nothing is flowing and wakes on demand: that wake takes microseconds. What we do not know: what it costs in a game, no published measurement puts a number on it, and our own instrument, which counts in milliseconds, is at least thirty times too coarse to see it. We report it because it is there, not because we know what it is worth.

data.name: Finding.Network.InterruptModerationTradeoff
data.value: Interrupt moderation is on for your network adapter. Microsoft advises turning it off only when the lowest possible latency is the goal, warning that it costs more CPU time; its documentation is about servers, and no published measurement puts a number on the effect in games. This is a trade-off, not a fault to fix. The scan measures how stable your network is, but it does not compare your adapter with and without this setting, so it cannot tell you what you would gain.

data.name: NonNuisance.Never.Voltage
data.value: DrDXT never writes a graphics card voltage: the card undervolt is a clock offset, not a voltage/frequency curve. On the processor, it only lowers the voltage, by 125 mV at most, and reads it back.

data.name: NonNuisance.Never.Firmware
data.value: DrDXT never writes to firmware, to the BIOS or to your card's VBIOS: it reads BIOS settings from Windows without changing them. For "Restart into the BIOS", it asks Windows, which sets that boot request itself.

data.name: NonNuisance.Never.KernelDriver
data.value: DrDXT installs no new driver on your machine; on your Undo, it can only put back a driver it had removed. It goes through the Windows APIs and your graphics vendor's own; if you installed PawnIO yourself, DrDXT loads into it only its own modules, built into DrDXT and checked against a pinned fingerprint before loading (to read and set the processor's power limit and voltage, and to read its temperature and the motherboard's fans).

data.name: NonNuisance.Never.SilentFan
data.value: DrDXT never leaves your card's fan at a fixed speed above 80 °C: from 80 °C, or if the temperature cannot be read, the fan returns to the card's own curve, and if DrDXT's administrator tool stops answering, the app returns it at once. A fixed speed is never below 40 %, nor below what the card aims for at that moment. Limit: if DrDXT stops entirely, the fixed speed stays until its next launch or a restart, and the card throttles itself as it heats.

data.name: SousTension.Refusee
data.value: Your BIOS refuses undervolting from Windows: "UnderVolt Protection" is enabled (the default). Nothing was changed. Two ways, in the BIOS: 1) OC menu, disable "UnderVolt Protection" (without SGX it protects nothing), then run the search again (guide 5.23). 2) Option not there (often hidden on MSI boards): lower the voltage in the BIOS itself. On MSI, OC menu, "CPU Lite Load": a lower mode gives less voltage; go down one step at a time, play a match or run ten minutes of load at each step, and go back up one step at the first crash. On other boards: "CPU Core Voltage" in adaptive mode with a negative offset, -30 mV to start.

data.name: SousTension.Refusee.ASRock
data.value: Your BIOS refuses undervolting from Windows: "UnderVolt Protection" is enabled (the default). Nothing was changed. On your ASRock board, lower the voltage in the BIOS itself (path given by ASRock support): 1) OC Tweaker > Voltage Configuration. 2) "CPU Core/Cache Voltage" in Offset Mode, negative offset: -30 mV to start. 3) F10 to save, then a match or ten minutes of load; at the first crash, go back to the previous offset.

data.name: SousTension.Refusee.ASUS
data.value: Your BIOS refuses undervolting from Windows: "UnderVolt Protection" is enabled (the default). Nothing was changed. On your ASUS board (ASUS 700 series BIOS manuals): 1) In the BIOS, F7 for advanced mode, Ai Tweaker > Tweaker's Paradise > "UnderVolt Protection": Disabled (without SGX it protects nothing). 2) F10 to save, then run the search again (guide 5.23). Or lower the voltage in the BIOS itself: Ai Tweaker > "SVID Behavior" to Typical or Best-Case, which give less voltage than Worst-Case or Intel's Fail Safe; one step at a time, a match or ten minutes of load at each step, and back to the previous step at the first crash.

data.name: SousTension.Refusee.MSI
data.value: Your BIOS refuses undervolting from Windows: "UnderVolt Protection" is enabled (the default). Nothing was changed. On your MSI board: 1) At startup, press Delete to enter the BIOS, then F7 for advanced mode, OC menu. 2) If "UnderVolt Protection" is there: set it to Disabled (without SGX it protects nothing), F10 to save, then run the search again (guide 5.23). 3) Otherwise (often hidden on MSI), lower the voltage in the BIOS itself: OC menu, "CPU Lite Load". A lower mode gives less voltage: go down one step at a time, play a match or run ten minutes of load at each step, and go back up one step at the first crash. F10 to save.

data.name: Finding.Memory.XmpOnSousLeKitAvecArrets
data.value: Overclock on, but below the kit speed, and unclean shutdowns in the last 90 days. Your RAM runs above the JEDEC standard speed: it is a memory overclock, by XMP/EXPO profile or manual setting, and the BIOS domain says which when it is readable; and Windows has restarted without a clean shutdown (long presses of the power button excluded; the breakdown, blue screens included, is in the stability report). DrDXT has not tested this setting and is not blaming it. Why go back to JEDEC: it is the only way to know whether this overclock crashes the machine. It tests stability, not performance. Stay on JEDEC for at least three times the usual gap between two shutdowns: for example, with one shutdown every nine days, a week without one can happen by chance. If the shutdowns stop over that time, the overclock becomes the most likely suspect. If they continue, the overclock is not the cause, but the modules are not cleared either. A memory test checks them faster than weeks of waiting: the one built into Windows (Windows + R, then mdsched.exe; it restarts the PC and keeps it busy during the test), whose result DrDXT then shows in the stability report, or MemTest86, which takes longer. Without restarting, the test in the Act section below checks a quarter of your memory in five minutes, but it cannot see the memory Windows itself uses: no error is not the same as a full test. Your RAM also runs below its kit's rated speed: the kit profile is not applied as is, often to stabilise. Run the memory test first before going back up to the kit speed.
